Fact check: AI LITERACY IN APPLIED CONTEXTS
A Talk for SUNY Morrisville Faculty
May 19, 2026


OPENING


I want to start with a simple observation.


When most people in higher education talk about AI literacy, they mean something like this: a student prompts a model, gets text back, and makes decisions about what to do with that output. The evidence of their thinking is in the conversation. The product is a document, an argument, a piece of writing.


That is the compositional case. And almost all of the AI literacy pedagogy being developed right now — the frameworks, the rubrics, the course guidelines — was built for that case.


I want to walk you around campus for a few minutes, because I don't think that describes your students.


STOP ONE: THE DAIRY FARM


Your students working in automated dairy operations are going to encounter a milking parlor that looks like this.


Robotic milking systems handle the milking. The cows come and go on their own schedule. The AI monitors each animal: milk yield, conductivity, milking frequency, body weight, reproductive status. The system makes feeding recommendations. It flags animals for attention. It surfaces patterns that suggest a cow needs follow-up.


Your student's job is not to milk the cow. It's to read the dashboard, evaluate the flag, and decide whether to act on it.


The system has already shaped the field of attention. Your student arrives after the dashboard has decided what looks important.


And that term — attention — is not accidental.


The architecture underneath many modern AI systems is literally called a transformer, built around what computer scientists call an attention mechanism: a way of weighting which signals matter most in a given context.


Humans do something similar. We constantly prioritize attention through training, instinct, experience, and judgment.


But now another attention system is entering the workflow before the human operator begins evaluating the situation.


The dashboard is not the situation. It is the model's interpretation of the situation.


Under what circumstances should your student override it? That's not a technical question. That's a literacy question.


STOP TWO: THE AUTO SHOP


Your automotive technology students are going to work in shops where the first thing that happens when a vehicle comes in is someone plugs in an OBD-II scanner.


The scanner reads the diagnostic trouble codes. AI-assisted diagnostic platforms cross-reference those codes against repair records for similar vehicles, group related codes, prioritize probable causes, and present a recommended repair sequence with confidence scores.


Your student sees the recommendation on a tablet.


The AI has already organized what looks important. Your student's attention is directed before their hands-on inspection begins.


They might run additional tests. They might catch something the scanner missed. But the workflow is: recommendation first, verification second — if at all.


What does it take to recognize when the recommendation is wrong? That's not a scanning skill. That's a judgment skill.


STOP THREE: THE GREENHOUSE


Your horticulture students are going to manage crops in environments where AI is already making autonomous decisions.


Irrigation systems adjust water delivery based on soil moisture sensors and weather data — without asking anyone. Climate control systems set temperature, humidity, and CO2 levels. Camera systems scan for disease and pest presence, flag anomalies, and recommend treatments.


The grower — your student — receives a report. An alert. A dashboard.


The system has often already acted before they see it.


What does fixation look like when the disease alert fires and attention goes to the flagged plant while the actual outbreak is two rows over? What does it cost when the dashboard declares the field healthy and your student stops looking?


In each of these three cases, the cognitive challenge is the same: the AI system increasingly organizes what the operator notices first.


THE COGNITIVE CHALLENGE


Human-factors researchers have documented recurring failure modes when operators work alongside automated systems. You see them in aviation, in clinical decision support, in process control:


Manual skill atrophy. Plan continuation bias. Vigilance decrement. Omission errors. Commission errors. Confirmation bias. Expectation-driven processing.


What these have in common is not complexity. They are all failures of attention — the operator's attention has been pre-organized by the system, and independent judgment has been displaced by cue-following.


Aviation addressed several of these through mandatory manual flying and scenario-based training under realistic conditions. The FAA can mandate that because the stakes are existential — plane crashes kill people.


Your students at Morrisville are not pilots. We do not need to train them to do everything manually as a backup.


But we do need to train them to maintain an independent model of the situation — to recognize when their own observation of the cow, the car, or the plant contradicts what the system is telling them, and to know what to do with that contradiction.


That is a practiced habit of judgment. It does not emerge from instruction about AI.


WHAT MAKES THIS ROUND DIFFERENT


Many earlier automation failures were more mechanically legible. The pump breaks. The sensor malfunctions. You can see it. You can trace it.


This round of AI-assisted automation is different in three ways.


First, the logic is opaque. The system makes a recommendation based on patterns it learned from large amounts of data. You cannot always ask it why and get a clear answer.


Second, it fails by being confidently wrong. AI can produce a plausible-looking recommendation that happens to be incorrect for your specific cow, your specific vehicle, your specific crop — and nothing in the interface signals that.


Third, introducing AI into automation may actually increase the cognitive demand on the human operator. The milking robot reduced physical labor. The AI-assisted milking system requires your student to constantly evaluate recommendations from a system they cannot fully see into, at scale, every day.


The issue is not simply that AI produces recommendations. The issue is that AI systems increasingly organize what the operator notices first — before the operator has had a chance to form an independent assessment.


WHAT AI LITERACY MEANS HERE


Not: teach students to use the tools.


Not: teach students about automation bias.


This: design courses where students practice the moment of judgment before compliance. Where the AI recommendation is sometimes wrong by design. Where they have to articulate why they're pausing. Where following the system blindly costs them something in simulation before it costs them something in the field.


Students need to learn to recognize the dashboard as model-generated rather than reality-generated. That is a different habit than spotting hallucinations in a text. It is the habit of maintaining epistemic separation between what the model surfaced and what is actually happening in the barn, the shop, or the greenhouse.


Your dairy students should encounter scenarios where the feeding algorithm has miscalculated and they have to catch it by reading the herd.


Your auto students should encounter vehicles where the scanner recommendation is wrong and their hands-on inspection is the only thing that catches it.


Your horticulture students should encounter disease alerts that are false positives — and silent outbreaks the system missed.


That's not a new course. That's a design principle you can embed in the courses you're already teaching.


AI literacy in applied fields is not primarily about producing content with AI. It is about preserving independent professional judgment while AI systems increasingly organize what appears important before humans even begin to think.


That is what AI literacy looks like at SUNY Morrisville.

Thought for 17s

I’ll separate the talk into checkable factual claims, verify them against public sources, and flag claims that are better framed as interpretive rather than settled fact.


Fact-check summary


Overall: mostly supportable, but several claims need narrower wording. The strongest parts are the dairy, greenhouse, transformer/attention, and automation-bias claims. The weakest parts are the auto-shop “confidence scores / recommendation first” specificity and the broad claim that most AI-literacy pedagogy is compositional.

#
Claim
Status
Notes
1
SUNY Morrisville is an applied college with relevant dairy, automotive, and horticulture programs.
Verified
Morrisville publicly lists automotive, horticulture, and applied hands-on programs; its dairy complex includes an electronically enhanced parlor and student-managed computer systems. (SUNY)
2
SUNY Morrisville has or is adding robotic dairy milkers.
Verified
Morrisville announced $1.36M for three robotic milkers at the Arnold R. Fisher Dairy Complex. (SUNY Morrisville)
3
Robotic milking systems allow cows to enter voluntarily/on their own schedule.
Verified
Public reporting describes robotic milking as a voluntary system where cows set their own milking schedule. (CNYBJ)
4
Robotic milking systems monitor milk yield, milking frequency, electrical conductivity, feed intake, and body weight.
Verified
Peer-reviewed and technical summaries support these variables; “reproductive status” is plausible but should be specified as activity/hormone or reproduction-related indicators, depending on the system. (PMC)
5
Robotic dairy systems can generate alerts for abnormal milk/cow conditions.
Verified
Automatic milking systems include control systems and alerts for deviations/abnormalities. (ScienceDirect)
6
Feeding recommendations are part of automated/robotic milking workflows.
Mostly verified
AMS changes how cows are fed and can deliver programmed concentrate feed at the milking station. “AI makes feeding recommendations” is stronger than the source; better: “software-managed feeding and recommendation systems increasingly shape feeding decisions.” (Dairy)
7
Transformers are AI architectures built around attention mechanisms.
Verified
The original Transformer paper explicitly proposes an architecture “based solely on attention mechanisms.” (arXiv)
8
“Attention” in transformers weights signals/tokens by contextual relevance.
Verified, with wording caution
Correct at a high level. Avoid implying transformer attention is psychologically equivalent to human attention. (arXiv)
9
OBD-II scanners read diagnostic trouble codes.
Verified
Standard automotive diagnostic workflow; sources on AI-assisted OBD-II tools explicitly discuss reading codes such as P0420. (AI Auto Repair Tools)
10
AI-assisted automotive diagnostic tools cross-reference repair databases and suggest likely causes/repair paths.
Mostly verified
Commercial/industry sources support guided testing, fix databases, and AI diagnostic insights. The exact language “confidence scores” and “recommendation first, verification second” should be softened unless tied to a specific product. (AI Auto Repair Tools)
11
Morrisville automotive students work with advanced diagnostics/onboard computer technologies.
Verified
Morrisville describes “leading-edge technology” in advanced diagnostics and facilities modeled on dealerships/body shops. (SUNY Morrisville)
12
AI/IoT greenhouse systems support irrigation, climate control, pest/disease detection, and optimization.
Verified
Recent review literature supports AI/IoT use in irrigation, climate control, fertigation, pest/disease detection, and optimization. (ScienceDirect)
13
Greenhouse systems may make autonomous decisions for climate, lighting, irrigation, etc.
Verified
Sensor/automation literature describes intelligent control making autonomous decisions for climate systems, lighting, and irrigation. (MDPI)
14
Practical deployment of advanced greenhouse AI is uneven/limited by integration, data, and computational constraints.
Important caveat
Your text implies broad current adoption. Better to say these systems are “emerging or increasingly used,” not universal. (ScienceDirect)
15
Automation bias includes omission and commission errors.
Verified
NASA and human-factors literature explicitly identify automation-related omission and commission errors. (Veriarch)
16
Automation bias is documented in aviation and clinical decision support.
Verified
Supported by NASA/aviation sources and healthcare AI/CDSS literature. (Veriarch)
17
Plan continuation bias is a recognized aviation human-factors concept.
Verified
SKYbrary defines it as continuing an original plan despite changing conditions; FAA materials connect it to CFIT risk. (Skybrary)
18
Vigilance decrement is a documented problem in automated monitoring.
Verified
Human-factors research supports vigilance decrement in automation-monitoring contexts. (movingforwardnetwork.org)
19
FAA/aviation guidance emphasizes maintaining manual flight proficiency.
Verified
FAA SAFO 17007 concerns manual flight operations proficiency and recommends maintaining/improving those skills. (Federal Aviation Administration)
20
“Aviation addressed several of these through mandatory manual flying.”
Needs revision
FAA guidance supports manual proficiency, but “mandatory manual flying” is too broad unless you cite a specific rule/operator policy. Safer: “aviation has addressed this partly through guidance, training, and policies to maintain manual-flight proficiency.” (Federal Aviation Administration)
21
AI systems can be opaque and can produce plausible but wrong recommendations.
Verified generally
Strongly supported for AI systems broadly and clinical decision support; for each applied domain, phrase as risk rather than universal property. (ScienceDirect)
22
AI-assisted automation can increase cognitive demands on operators.
Supported, but interpretive
Human-factors literature supports that automation can shift work from action to monitoring and create new error modes. Your dairy-specific version is plausible but not directly proven by the sources found. (ScienceDirect)
23
“Most AI literacy pedagogy right now was built for the compositional case.”
Unverified / too broad
This is rhetorically plausible, but I would not state it as fact without a literature review. Safer: “Much visible AI-literacy pedagogy, especially in writing-intensive contexts, focuses on prompting, evaluating, and revising generated text.”
24
“AI literacy in applied fields is about preserving independent professional judgment.”
Interpretive thesis
Not a factual claim; it is your argument. It is well-aligned with automation-bias literature but should be presented as a pedagogical claim, not an established consensus.

Recommended wording changes


Replace “almost all AI literacy pedagogy” with “much of the visible AI-literacy guidance in higher education.”

Replace “AI-assisted diagnostic platforms … present a recommended repair sequence with confidence scores” with “some AI-assisted diagnostic platforms combine trouble codes with repair databases or guided testing to prioritize likely causes and suggest next diagnostic steps.”

Replace “Aviation addressed several of these through mandatory manual flying” with “Aviation has addressed related risks partly through training and guidance aimed at maintaining manual-flight proficiency.”

Replace “AI is already making autonomous decisions” in greenhouse section with “AI- and sensor-driven systems are increasingly capable of autonomous or semi-autonomous control decisions.”

Keep the dashboard/model/reality distinction. That is the strongest conceptual through-line and is well supported by automation-bias literature.
